Adding a few clarifications regarding the competition:

  • Kaggle Benchmarks proxy quota & public datasets: It is not the intent of the Benchmarks proxy quota to be used for non-benchmarking work; however, we will not penalize participants who have already used it (no action is needed on earlier submissions). Public community datasets on Kaggle (including those generated via the proxy) are fine to train on.
  • Self-generated data: Self-generated training data (within reasonable cost, as noted earlier) does not need to be made public, so there is no publication deadline for it.
  • Public pre-trained weights: Additionally, model weights (such as LoRA adapters) that are publicly available to all participants on Kaggle are fine to use.

@martinosmani @rarjunthilak

Thank you!

comments.content:
Thanks for the questions! Here is some clarification on these points:

  • Data generation: This is intended to be an ML prediction competition, not a data generation competition. Effectively "buying" more training data via token spend beyond the value of a possible prize ($5k) would be considered unreasonable.
  • Kaggle Benchmarks quota: The Benchmarks proxy quota is reserved for benchmark evaluation runs, not for generating competition training data please see the answer below
  • Winner license: Yes. An OSI-approved open source license for the write-up and documentation is acceptable.
  • Existing public datasets: Existing public community datasets on Kaggle are fine to train on.

comments.content: @martynaplomecka — a follow-up on the Benchmarks proxy quota, because the earlier answers cover training data and I want to be sure about evaluation use. We would like to use the proxy only to test an already-trained 18-way classifier: generate fresh passages from the candidate models on new prompts, keep them private and sealed, and use them only for scoring (never as training rows, never published as training data). Is that within "benchmark evaluation runs"? If yes, we would do it through a Benchmarks task (kaggle benchmarks tasks run) rather than ad-hoc calls, keep the spend well under the daily quota, and say so in the write-up. If you would rather we avoid it entirely, we will use only our 7/18 free-generation bench. Thanks!

firstMessage.content:
Hi @martynaplomecka @yanyao23,

The same few rules questions are spread across many threads, none answered yet. Here is a quick summary, plus a few specific points, so one reply can settle them for everyone.

Already asked (still open):

  • Is generated training data allowed, and at what cost? Passages generated from the 18 models through paid APIs, and whether publishing them makes them OK under §2.6: 749613, 751011, 751294, 751954, 750216. The fairness debate is in 749447 (the most-voted topic).

  • Can the Kaggle Benchmarks quota be used to generate data? 750038, 750512.

  • Can solutions train on the community datasets already published on Kaggle? 751954, 751544.

  • Were the gemini-3.7-flash labels generated before Google started routing 3.7 requests to 3.8 (Oct 8)? 751954.

  • How is the test set laid out? (how many models answer each test prompt, and how public and private are split): 750768, 751802, 750213.

Specific questions:

  1. Published generated data: suppose a participant generates passages by calling the candidate models' APIs (paid, or through the Kaggle Benchmarks quota) and publishes the full dataset as a public Kaggle Dataset (e.g. CC BY 4.0) before using it. Does that satisfy §2.6.a whatever the generation cost? Is there a deadline for publishing, such as the Jan 6 entry deadline?

  2. Unpublished generated data: can API-generated data that is not published qualify under the §2.6.b Reasonableness Standard? If so, roughly what total spend counts as "minimal cost": tens, hundreds or thousands of dollars?

  3. Kaggle Benchmarks model proxy: is it fine to use the free proxy quota to generate training passages for this competition?

  4. Winner licence: the rules header says CC BY 4.0, while §2.5.a.1 asks for an OSI-approved licence. Is MIT or Apache-2.0 for code, plus CC BY 4.0 for the write-up, acceptable?

  5. Test-time inference: may a submission notebook use relationships between hidden-test passages (for example, clustering or pseudo-labelling inside the notebook), fully automated with no human input?

Even short yes/no answers would help a lot of teams plan the rest of the competition.

Thanks!

first_message.content:
Hi @martynaplomecka @yanyao23,

The same few rules questions are spread across many threads, none answered yet. Here is a quick summary, plus a few specific points, so one reply can settle them for everyone.

Already asked (still open):

  • Is generated training data allowed, and at what cost? Passages generated from the 18 models through paid APIs, and whether publishing them makes them OK under §2.6: 749613, 751011, 751294, 751954, 750216. The fairness debate is in 749447 (the most-voted topic).

  • Can the Kaggle Benchmarks quota be used to generate data? 750038, 750512.

  • Can solutions train on the community datasets already published on Kaggle? 751954, 751544.

  • Were the gemini-3.7-flash labels generated before Google started routing 3.7 requests to 3.8 (Oct 8)? 751954.

  • How is the test set laid out? (how many models answer each test prompt, and how public and private are split): 750768, 751802, 750213.

Specific questions:

  1. Published generated data: suppose a participant generates passages by calling the candidate models' APIs (paid, or through the Kaggle Benchmarks quota) and publishes the full dataset as a public Kaggle Dataset (e.g. CC BY 4.0) before using it. Does that satisfy §2.6.a whatever the generation cost? Is there a deadline for publishing, such as the Jan 6 entry deadline?

  2. Unpublished generated data: can API-generated data that is not published qualify under the §2.6.b Reasonableness Standard? If so, roughly what total spend counts as "minimal cost": tens, hundreds or thousands of dollars?

  3. Kaggle Benchmarks model proxy: is it fine to use the free proxy quota to generate training passages for this competition?

  4. Winner licence: the rules header says CC BY 4.0, while §2.5.a.1 asks for an OSI-approved licence. Is MIT or Apache-2.0 for code, plus CC BY 4.0 for the write-up, acceptable?

  5. Test-time inference: may a submission notebook use relationships between hidden-test passages (for example, clustering or pseudo-labelling inside the notebook), fully automated with no human input?

Even short yes/no answers would help a lot of teams plan the rest of the competition.

Thanks!
